newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Greek-Turkish concert in Cyprus causes controversy.
newsitem.headline: Greek-Turkish concert in Cyprus causes controversy.

text.p: Greek and Turkish musicians will sing for peace on the divided island of Cyprus on Monday in a concert which has struck a note of discord with factions in both communities.
Pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece will play in U.N.-policed no man's land in the capital Nicosia to an audience split by war, bad memories and deep mistrust.
"It is a really noble cause," said Waldemar Rokoszewski, spokesman for the United Nations peacekeeping force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, which is sponsoring the event.
"People will be getting together, especially the young generation of Cypriots who have been apart for such a long time and in fact do not know each other," he told Reuters.

The Greek Cypriot-led government has expressed its support for the event, as have leftist parties and organisations in both the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. Nationalist parties and groups have opposed it.
Concert tickets are free, and the United Nations has allocated 3,000 to each community. Security in the concert area will be the responsibility of the United Nations.

Some Greek Cypriots are angry that the concert is being held while the memory is still raw of the killings of two of their fellow countrymen by Turks or Turkish Cypriots on the ceasefire line last year.
"This is grossly insensitive and an insult to the families of our heroes and us," said George Hadjicostas, head of the Cyprus Motorcyclists Federation (CMF).
"Let's go and spit on him," say CMF posters which started appearing in the Greek Cypriot part of the capital this week, referring to Rouvas.
The CMF is organising a protest on the night of the concert.
"We don't need Rouvas to tell us what our problem is. Our problem is not AIDS and drugs. Our problem is with the Turkish occupation," said Hadjicostas.
The concert is one of several events planned by the United Nations in an attempt to boost grassroots contacts between the two sides which have been virtually non-existent since 1974.

Turkish troops invaded northern Cyprus in July of that year in response to a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Attempts to reunite the island under a federal umbrella have floundered.
On the northern side of the divide, a far-right group, Turk-Bir, issued a statement calling on all its members not to go to the concert.
It said the group had information that "Greek Cypriot fanatics" were preparing for trouble and provocations.
Despite the concerns, Turkish Cypriots queued for tickets.
"I will go to the concert," said Yusuf Ersoy, 20, a Turkish Cypriot university student.

"It's a good organisation, a positive step. It will give young people from both sides the chance to come together. But people with ill intentions may create troubles. I hope measures are taken against these."
In the south the United Nations had to expand its ticket distribution network because of the low demand.
"I don't want to spit on him (Rouvas), I just don't like his music," said Greek Cypriot businesswoman Yiota Christodoulides, 27.
She said she would not have minded going to a bicommunal concert if it had been a Greek musician of her choice.
"I don't mind a Turkish singer being there," Christodoulides said. "They aren't all bad."
